articles.title: Do tokenized treasuries actually trade? I checked 29 RWA tokens on-chain
articles.description: "Tokenization makes illiquid assets liquid" is the line in almost every real-world-asset (RWA) pitch deck. A token can move 24/7, so the asset must be liquid, right? Being transferable is not the same as being traded. So I looked at what actually happens on-chain. I took 29 tokenized treasuries, money-market funds, credit funds, gold tokens and two real-estate tokens, and counted transfers over 30 days using public block-explorer data (Blockscout). The question for each token: do holders actually pass it to each other, or does it mostly get issued and redeemed by the issuer? How I measured it For every token, over a 30-day window (scan date: 28 October 2026): Holders: addresses holding a balance. Top-10 share: how much of the supply the 10 largest holders own. Mints and redemptions: tokens created or destroyed by the issuer. This is primary-market activity. Secondary transfers: transfers from one holder to another holder, which is the closest on-chain proxy for a secondary market. Unique wallets involved in those secondary transfers. One caveat up front: a holder-to-holder transfer is not always a trade. It can be a custodian moving between its own wallets, or a DeFi contract. So treat these numbers as an upper bound for real secondary trading. What I found 1. Gold tokens behave like normal crypto assets. XAUT and PAXG each have tens of thousands of holders (about 63,000 and 92,000) and about 1,500 holder-to-holder transfers each in 30 days (the scan's cap, so the real number is higher) across hundreds of wallets. They are widely held and freely moved. 2. Yield tokens built for DeFi move a lot too. USDY (Ondo) and syrupUSDC (Maple) each showed more than 1,200 secondary transfers across roughly 300 wallets. These are designed to plug into DeFi, and it shows. 3. Many institutional treasury and credit funds barely trade between holders. A few examples from the same 30 days: Token Holders Top-10 share Mints Secondary transfers Wallets involved BUIDL (Ethereum) 55 86% 647 34 17 WTGXX 74 99% 135 26 15 OUSG 52 95% 11 12 5 JTRSY 20 100% 4 USYC 25 2 BUIDL is the clearest case. On Ethereum it was minted 647 times in the window, but holders passed it to each other only 34 times. Activity is almost all primary: investors subscribe and redeem with the issuer, not with each other. That is by design for a permissioned fund with whitelisted holders. 4. Some tokens show no secondary activity at all. Benji (Franklin Templeton) on Base, Arbitrum and Polygon had between 3 and 8 holders on each chain, plenty of mints, and zero holder-to-holder transfers. The two real-estate tokens in the sample had 12 and 2 holders and no secondary transfers either. 5. Concentration is the norm. In 19 of the 29 tokens, the 10 largest holders own 95% or more of the supply. So, is tokenization making assets liquid? For gold and DeFi-native yield tokens, yes: there is real movement between many independent wallets. For most tokenized funds, the honest answer is "not yet". The token makes settlement and record-keeping easier and lets eligible investors subscribe and redeem faster. But secondary liquidity still depends on things the blockchain cannot create: enough eligible holders, a venue that is allowed to match them, and someone willing to make a market. If you are an issuer, "we'll be liquid because we're on-chain" is not a plan. Look at who is allowed to hold the token, where it can legally trade, and who will provide liquidity on day one. If you are an investor, check the on-chain numbers yourself before assuming you can exit early. The redemption terms with the issuer usually matter more than the chain. Check it yourself The full index with every token, its holders and its secondary activity: Floatscore RWA Liquidity Index A weekly summary of holder and supply changes for the largest RWA tokens: RWA Weekly on Telegram To scan any other ERC-20 token on Ethereum, Polygon, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism or Gnosis with your own time window, I published the scanner as a pay-per-use tool: RWA Token Liquidity Scanner Data from public block explorers, scanned on 28 October 2026 over a 30-day window. Counts above 1,500 were capped by the scan. This is data, not investment advice.
